KillerStrike article 4303 evidence and coverage
Source: https://threatmon.io/killerstrike-inside-an-open-source-windows-rat/
Saved summary was supplemented with the full HTML and 17 original-resolution
screenshots, stored in scratch. There are no HTML pre/code blocks. Code is
shown in screenshots; figures 12-15 were checked against recovered source.
Figure 6 also contains an operator PowerShell DownloadString/Invoke-Expression
example, without a supplied payload URL. No payload was invented for it.

Artifact identity and retrieval
Figure 1 names https://gitlab.com/fsec-vaul/killerstrike . Figure 2 shows
revision 9ca64bce. Forager recovered that revision's source archive from
https://gitlab.com/fsec-vaul/killerstrike/-/archive/9ca64bce/killerstrike-9ca64bce.tar.gz
The source functions and line structure match the article screenshots.
The archive is original downloaded source, not the article's agent.exe, and
was not compiled or executed. Its Forager sidecar remains in recovery/generic,
outside testdata. The failed hash download left a GitLab HTML response, which
was moved to recovery/gitlab-page.html and excluded from the sample set.
The sole sample is testdata/hostile/killerstrike-9ca64bce.tar.gz.
Archive SHA-256: 9109d576a31189939c04b63e3e2d87f41b8186b472e3e4465ccf69ec66206052

Figure 17 supplies agent.exe SHA-256:
507023cdb4047baf075b0030ae42513bf76b115f379d28ca07d310d1b3c9d02e
Figure 16 supplies the same 511924-byte PE64 agent's other hashes:
MD5 e81434ff5640400eb1347f6b25f7a8ba
SHA-1 4e36e69390afe64e4f85f09c766961ee2435fa92
Forager tried the URL with SHA-256, then MalwareBazaar, Triage and Malshare;
none provided matching executable bytes. A zero-detection AntiScan result
is not a benign comparison: the scanned file is the RAT under examination.
All three article file hashes are retained in testdata/SHA256.
9ca64bce is a Git commit abbreviation, not a file hash or package version.
PURLS records KillerStrike by name only. The article calls it an alpha release
but supplies no package ecosystem, release version or versioned coordinate.
No source-package PURL is inferred from the executable or commit.

Indicators and context
ENDPOINTS contains 127.0.0.1: the supplied server default is
http://127.0.0.1:4444. This is a laboratory/default address, not public deployed
attacker infrastructure. gitlab.com and t.me are shared distribution services;
the specific repository and Telegram promotion are contextual URLs, not a
claim that the shared hosts are malicious. The pinned CoreveilCrypter channel
is unrelated to the analyzed artifact. AntiScan, Google, MSYS2, GitHub package
downloads and browser-history addresses are analyst/lab context, excluded.
The package download screenshot labels the MSYS2 executable as interesting,
not malicious, as the article explicitly explains.

Default artifacts (corroboration only, never required to convict)
Service OptiDiagSvc; display name Optimized Diagnostics Service;
C:\Program Files\Optimized Diagnostics\; OptiDiagSvc.exe; OptDiagCore.dll.
Configuration permits these names to change. The default host uses routes
/api/agents/register, /api/agents/result and /api/agents/<id>/files/upload.
The other file-transfer route is /api/agents/<id>/files/<remote>.

Detection changes and limits
- Distinct hostile AMSI clean-result and ETW return-zero patch detections use
  structured GetProcAddress provenance, onward passing of the resolved
  address, patch bytes, VirtualProtect calls and native memcpy calls in the
  same file. These are static patch evidence, not proof of runtime success.
  Names of helpers, services, DLLs, C2 hosts and endpoints do not gate them.
- Existing return-zero byte-array observation now covers both 31 C0 C3 and
  33 C0 C3 encodings. The AMSI array checks a sixth stack-argument load, a
  zero store through the result pointer, and return in the same initializer.
- CLR ExecuteInDefaultAppDomain is matched as a call, with member spelling
  normalized by facts; existing Go handling is retained without duplication.
- WinHTTP certificate-ignore masks must be passed by the same local variable
  to WINHTTP_OPTION_SECURITY_FLAGS in the same statement block.
- A bare Google Chromekey1 identifier was moved from credential-access to
  neutral crypto/key/representation and made notable. Both narrow and wide
  observations moved; all five explicit consuming references were updated.
  Broad objective-directory selectors intentionally no longer count a bare
  key name as evidence of credential access. No nearby rule gained alternatives.
- Cursor polling moved to hardware/input/mouse/position. The replacement
  requires two actual GetCursorPos calls and no longer claims sandbox evasion.
  The removed sleep-plus-cursor objective had no exact consumers. Its broad
  sandbox-directory exclusion no longer treats ordinary polling as a sandbox.
- The browser credential-path pair was already in fs/path/password-store;
  it now requires a parsed literal and is notable. Its old suspicious finding
  came entirely from a comment explicitly denying credential collection.
  The direct exfiltration consumer retains the same reference and cannot be
  triggered by that comment anymore.

Coverage gaps
The original PE is unavailable, so native compiled-byte coverage is not
claimed. The recovered archive yields two distinct hostile patch behaviors;
we do not raise ordinary service creation, capture APIs, network requests or
browser database access to hostile to reach a quota. Direct SQLite record
parsing in browsers.c is not detected by SQL-query-specific theft rules.
AMSI/ETW and CLR/WinHTTP are intrinsically Windows techniques; source-language
scopes allow renamed implementations while keeping the actual OS boundary.
No claim of successful App-Bound v20 recovery or reusable cookie theft is made.

Verification
Cleave facts were saved for clrhost.c and the archive, including text,
structured calls/literals and decoded layers exposed by facts. Original
source was reviewed for the actual patch, CLR and WinHTTP operations.
Two positive C/C++ fixtures (including renamed helpers and 33 C0 XOR) are
registered in testdata/expectations.toml. Sixteen controls are in cleave's
fixtures/killerstrike-controls, outside the feed sample set. Controls check
references, ordinary copying, absent writes, wrong exports, missing return
instructions, comments, cursor polling, three language key references, CLR
calls versus strings, and TLS mask binding. Reports are saved in scratch.

Directory/reference audit: no new taxonomy leaf was added. The source-literal
leaf remains at its existing 100-rule budget by representing the clean-result
array as one structural observation. Existing ancestor selectors were audited;
Windows-only key observations cannot satisfy Unix-only source controls.

Final atomscan: sole hostile-tier archive passed, with two hostile traits
(AMSI clean-result patch and ETW return-zero patch). All 18 focused fixture
checks passed. No recovered executable or successful v20 decryption is claimed.
